title: Lactose tolerance · LCT/MCM6
summary: The rs4988235 variant upstream of the lactase gene (in an MCM6 intron, often written -13910C>T) is the main determinant of adult lactase persistence in people of European ancestry. Carrying at least one A allele (the forward-strand equivalent of the persistence T allele) keeps lactase expression switched on into adulthood, so dairy is usually well tolerated. The linked variant rs182549 (-22018, T allele) travels with it and supports the same interpretation.

interpretations.GG: Two copies of the ancestral G allele, the genotype associated with lactase non-persistence: lactase production typically declines after childhood, and larger servings of milk are more likely to cause bloating, gas, or loose stools. Tolerance varies a lot in practice, and fermented or low-lactose dairy is often handled comfortably. In some non-European populations, separate persistence variants not covered here can keep lactase active despite a GG result.
interpretations.AG: One copy of the A allele (the lactase-persistence allele). Lactase expression is generally maintained into adulthood, and most people with this genotype digest ordinary amounts of dairy without symptoms.
interpretations.AA: Two copies of the A allele, the genotype associated with full lactase persistence. Lactase continues to be produced in adulthood and dairy is typically well tolerated. Digestive symptoms after dairy in AA carriers usually have other explanations.

interpretations.CC: Two copies of the ancestral C allele at the linked -22018 site, consistent with lactase non-persistence. This variant is almost always inherited together with rs4988235, so the two results usually agree.
interpretations.CT: One copy of the T allele at the linked -22018 site, consistent with maintained adult lactase activity. This variant travels on the same haplotype as rs4988235 and mainly serves to confirm that result.
interpretations.TT: Two copies of the T allele at the linked -22018 site, consistent with full lactase persistence and comfortable dairy digestion for most carriers.

title: Alcohol flush reaction · ALDH2
summary: ALDH2 rs671 (Glu504Lys, ALDH2*2) largely inactivates the enzyme that clears acetaldehyde, the toxic first breakdown product of alcohol. The A allele, common in East Asian populations and rare elsewhere, is associated with facial flushing, nausea, and rapid heartbeat after drinking, and in people who drink heavily despite flushing, with substantially higher odds of esophageal cancer.

interpretations.GG: Two copies of the G (Glu504) allele: fully active ALDH2. Acetaldehyde is cleared at the typical rate and the classic alcohol flush reaction is not expected from this gene.
interpretations.AG: One copy of the A (Lys504) allele. Because the enzyme works as a tetramer, one inactive copy reduces ALDH2 activity far more than half, and most carriers flush and feel unwell after alcohol. Studies associate heavy drinking in AG carriers with several-fold higher odds of esophageal squamous cell cancer compared with GG heavy drinkers; carriers who drink little or not at all do not show this excess. This is one factor among many in cancer risk.
interpretations.AA: Two copies of the A (Lys504) allele: very little ALDH2 activity. Even small amounts of alcohol typically cause strong flushing and discomfort, and most AA carriers drink rarely, which in practice limits alcohol-related harm. Acetaldehyde accumulates markedly when alcohol is consumed.

title: Alcohol metabolism speed · ADH1B
summary: ADH1B rs1229984 (His48Arg) changes how fast alcohol is converted to acetaldehyde in the liver. The T allele (His48, the ADH1B*2 form, common in East Asia and present at low frequency elsewhere) encodes an enzyme that is roughly 40-fold faster in vitro. Faster conversion produces a brief acetaldehyde surge that makes drinking less pleasant, and the His48 allele is consistently associated with lower average alcohol intake and lower odds of alcohol use disorder.

interpretations.CC: Two copies of the C (Arg48) allele, the most common genotype in European and African populations: standard-speed ADH1B. Alcohol is converted to acetaldehyde at the typical rate, and this gene contributes no unusual push toward or away from drinking.
interpretations.CT: One copy of the fast T (His48) allele. Alcohol is oxidized to acetaldehyde noticeably faster, which on average is associated with drinking less and with lower odds of alcohol dependence compared with CC carriers. Behavior and environment remain far larger factors.
interpretations.TT: Two copies of the fast T (His48) allele, the most common genotype in East Asian populations. Rapid conversion of alcohol to acetaldehyde tends to make drinking less rewarding, and this genotype shows the strongest average association with lower alcohol intake and lower odds of alcohol use disorder at this gene.

title: Iron overload (C282Y) · HFE
summary: HFE rs1800562 (C282Y) is the main variant behind hereditary hemochromatosis, a recessive tendency to absorb too much dietary iron, which over decades can affect the liver, joints, and other organs. About 1 in 200 people of northern European ancestry carries two copies, but most who do never develop iron-overload disease: in a large cohort roughly 28% of male and about 1% of female homozygotes developed documented iron-overload-related disease. This is carrier-style information, not a health assessment.

interpretations.GG: No copies of the C282Y (A) allele. No increased iron-loading tendency from this variant, though the milder H63D variant (reported separately) and non-HFE causes are not excluded.
interpretations.AG: One copy of the C282Y (A) allele: a carrier. Carriers absorb slightly more iron on average but almost never develop iron overload from this alone (a compound effect is possible when combined with H63D). Mainly relevant as family-planning information, since children could inherit two copies if the other parent is also a carrier.
interpretations.AA: Two copies of the C282Y (A) allele, the genotype found in most people with hereditary hemochromatosis. Iron absorption is increased, but penetrance is limited: many homozygotes, especially women, maintain normal iron levels lifelong, while roughly a quarter of male homozygotes eventually develop iron-overload-related problems. Iron status is easily checked with routine blood tests (ferritin, transferrin saturation), which is worth mentioning to a clinician — this report describes an inherited tendency, not current iron levels.

citations.label: Allen et al., N Engl J Med 2008

title: Iron overload (H63D) · HFE
summary: HFE rs1799945 (H63D) is the milder of the two common hemochromatosis variants. On its own it rarely causes meaningful iron overload, even with two copies; it matters mainly in combination with C282Y (compound heterozygosity), and even then most carriers stay well. Around a quarter of people of European ancestry carry at least one G (Asp63) allele.

interpretations.CC: No copies of the H63D (G) allele. No iron-loading contribution from this variant; the separate C282Y report covers the higher-impact HFE variant.
interpretations.CG: One copy of the H63D (G) allele, a common finding of little consequence by itself. Its main relevance is in combination with one C282Y allele (compound heterozygosity), which modestly raises average iron measures, though iron-overload disease remains uncommon even then.
interpretations.GG: Two copies of the H63D (G) allele. Average iron measures run slightly higher, but iron-overload disease attributable to this genotype alone is rare. As with C282Y, actual iron status is a blood-test question rather than a genetic one.

citations.label: Allen et al., N Engl J Med 2008

title: Bilirubin processing · UGT1A1
summary: UGT1A1 rs887829 tags reduced activity of the enzyme that conjugates bilirubin for excretion; the T allele travels almost perfectly with the UGT1A1*28 promoter repeat behind Gilbert syndrome. Two T copies are associated with mildly elevated unconjugated bilirubin — a benign trait carried by roughly 10% of Europeans that can show up as slight yellowing of the eyes during fasting, illness, or stress, and as a flagged bilirubin value on routine blood panels.

interpretations.CC: Two copies of the C allele: typical UGT1A1 activity and typical bilirubin levels, with no Gilbert-pattern tendency from this locus.
interpretations.CT: One copy of the T allele. Average bilirubin runs slightly higher than in CC carriers but usually stays within the normal range; noticeable effects are uncommon.
interpretations.TT: Two copies of the T allele, the genotype associated with Gilbert syndrome: unconjugated bilirubin is on average roughly double that of CC carriers and can rise further with fasting or illness, occasionally causing mild, harmless yellowing of the eyes. Gilbert syndrome is benign — some studies even associate the higher bilirubin with slightly favorable cardiovascular markers — but it is worth knowing because reduced UGT1A1 activity also slows the processing of certain medications (for example irinotecan), something prescribers can take into account.

citations.label: Bosma et al., N Engl J Med 1995
Johnson et al., Hum Mol Genet 2009

title: Bitter taste perception · TAS2R38
summary: TAS2R38 rs713598 (Ala49Pro) is the lead variant of the classic taster/non-taster difference for PTC/PROP-type bitter compounds, which include the glucosinolates in cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli, kale, and Brussels sprouts. The G allele (Pro49, part of the taster PAV haplotype) is associated with perceiving these compounds as strongly bitter, which in some studies nudges vegetable preference and intake.

interpretations.CC: Two copies of the C (Ala49) allele, tagging the non-taster (AVI-type) receptor. PTC/PROP-class bitter compounds taste weak or absent, and cruciferous vegetables tend to taste milder. Two other linked positions in TAS2R38 fine-tune the phenotype, so perception still varies.
interpretations.CG: One taster (G/Pro49) and one non-taster (C/Ala49) allele: intermediate bitterness perception on average, with wide individual variation influenced by the other linked TAS2R38 positions and by experience.
interpretations.GG: Two copies of the G (Pro49) allele, tagging the taster (PAV-type) receptor. PTC/PROP-class compounds taste distinctly bitter, and on average GG carriers rate cruciferous vegetables as more bitter; whether that changes what anyone actually eats is mostly down to habit and preparation.

title: Celiac disease HLA background · HLA-DQA1
summary: Celiac disease, an immune reaction to gluten, occurs almost exclusively in people carrying the HLA-DQ2.5 or DQ8 molecules. rs2187668 is a well-validated tag for the DQ2.5 haplotype (HLA-DQA1*05:01–DQB1*02:01), which is present in around 90% of people with celiac disease. The genetics are far more useful for ruling out than ruling in: about a quarter of Europeans carry DQ2.5, yet only a few percent of carriers ever develop celiac disease.

interpretations.CC: No copies of the DQ2.5 tag allele. This makes the highest-risk celiac HLA background unlikely, though it does not exclude DQ8 or the less common DQ2.2, which this single variant does not capture — so it cannot fully rule celiac disease out on its own.
interpretations.CT: One copy of the T allele, tagging one DQ2.5 haplotype — the necessary immune background carried by most people with celiac disease. Carrying it is common (roughly a quarter of Europeans) and by itself means only a modestly elevated lifetime chance, on the order of a few percent. Persistent gut symptoms are a question for a clinician regardless of genotype.
interpretations.TT: Two copies of the T allele, consistent with a double dose of the DQ2.5 risk haplotype. Studies associate DQ2.5 homozygosity with the highest HLA-related celiac risk (several-fold above single-copy carriers), yet even here most carriers never develop celiac disease. This result describes an inherited immune background, one predisposing factor among several, not a statement about whether celiac disease is present.

title: Norovirus resistance (secretor status) · FUT2
summary: FUT2 rs601338 (Trp143Ter) determines secretor status: whether ABO-type sugar antigens are displayed on the gut lining, where common norovirus strains use them to attach. Two copies of the stop allele (A) make a person a non-secretor — about 20% of Europeans — which in challenge and outbreak studies is associated with strong resistance to Norwalk (GI.1) virus and to many globally dominant GII.4 stomach-bug strains. Non-secretors can still catch other norovirus genotypes.

interpretations.GG: Two functional FUT2 copies: a secretor. Gut-lining cells display the sugar antigens that Norwalk-type noroviruses bind, so susceptibility to these common winter vomiting bugs is typical. Secretor status also modestly shapes gut microbiome composition and average vitamin B12 levels in population studies.
interpretations.AG: One stop (A) allele and one working copy: still a secretor, since one functional FUT2 copy is enough to display the attachment antigens. Susceptibility to common norovirus strains is essentially the same as GG.
interpretations.AA: Two stop (A) alleles: a non-secretor. Without the attachment antigens on the gut lining, Norwalk (GI.1) virus infection was essentially absent in non-secretors in challenge studies, and resistance extends to many common GII.4 strains — a rare example of near-complete genetic protection. Other norovirus genotypes can still infect non-secretors, so this is not blanket immunity to stomach bugs. Non-secretor status has also been associated with slightly higher average B12 levels and, in some studies, modestly higher odds of Crohn's disease.

title: Liver fat tendency · PNPLA3
summary: PNPLA3 rs738409 (Ile148Met) is the strongest and most replicated common variant for non-alcoholic fatty liver. Each G (Met148) allele is associated with higher liver fat content — roughly doubled in GG carriers in the discovery study — and with higher odds of liver inflammation in both metabolic and alcohol-related liver disease. The association is strongly amplified by adiposity and alcohol intake, and correspondingly small in lean, low-alcohol contexts.

interpretations.CC: Two copies of the C (Ile148) allele: no added liver-fat tendency from this variant. Liver fat remains driven mainly by weight, metabolic health, and alcohol intake.
interpretations.CG: One copy of the G (Met148) allele, carried by roughly a third of people of European ancestry and more in Hispanic populations. Associated on average with modestly higher liver fat and somewhat higher odds of fatty liver, an effect that mostly surfaces alongside excess weight or regular alcohol use.
interpretations.GG: Two copies of the G (Met148) allele. Associated on average with about twice the liver fat of CC carriers and with higher odds of progressing from simple fatty liver to inflammation, particularly in combination with obesity or heavier drinking. This is a tendency, not a finding about the liver itself: many GG carriers have normal livers, and weight and alcohol remain the dominant, modifiable factors.
